studies.title: Four Lines Of Denial
studies.meaning: Four lines, and every one of them removes something. He is one, using a word for unity that Arabic uses of nothing else in this position. He is the one turned to for everything and needing nothing. He did not father and was not fathered, which closes both directions of descent. And nothing is equal to Him. Nothing positive is described at all, which the classical readers treat as the surah's method.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The sources report that people asked the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to describe his Lord, to say what He was made of and who His ancestors were, and that this surah was the answer. The reports differ over who asked. Arabia's gods had genealogies and territories, so a question about lineage was the natural first question to put.

keyTerms.note: A different word from the ordinary numeral for one. It is used in negative sentences to mean not anyone at all, so applying it positively here says a oneness that admits no second of any kind.
From a root meaning to head toward something and also to be solid with no hollow. Classical readers gather both: the one everyone turns to for need, and the one with nothing empty in Him.
The word used of a marriage partner of matching standing, and of anything comparable in worth. Denying it removes not only rivals but peers, so no scale exists on which a comparison could be made.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian gods were family. The three named in another surah were called daughters of a higher god, shrines were inherited, and a deity belonged to a place and a people. Asking about a god's parentage was not an insult; it was how you found out whose god it was. The surah's third line answers that question by refusing the whole category.
studies.didYouKnow: The early collections keep a report that this surah is equal to a third of the Quran. Another says a man who repeated it all night was told his love for it would bring him into the garden. It is four short lines. The classical explanation of the arithmetic is that the Quran's subject matter divides into three, and one of the three is this.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Describing God by denial keeps the description from turning into a picture. That is the surah's whole strategy. Every positive image a person forms would be drawn from something created. Each line here removes one such image before it can settle. The result is a definition that cannot be pictured and can still be recited by a child. That is why it became the shortest complete answer in the tradition.

crossReferences.why: States the same denial of any likeness and then attaches two attributes to it in the same line.
Uses the same technique at greater length, defining by what is denied rather than by what is pictured.
Answers the same claim about descent at length, with the heavens described as nearly splitting at it.

studies.applyIt: Say these four lines once and then try to notice what picture your mind supplied anyway. Everyone supplies one: a light, a direction, a presence somewhere above. Do not fight it. The surah works by removing pictures one at a time, and you cannot remove one you have not caught yourself making.
studies.explainEasier: God tells his messenger to say this. He is God, the only one. Everyone turns to him, and he needs nothing. He has no children and no parents. There is nothing at all like him.
